new_statements.quote: Koenoem is a tone language. It has three basic register tones. In Koenoem, tone is contrastive in that words that have the same orthographical representation are differentiated by the tone i.e. tonal differences bring about a change in the meaning of the affected words. Examples of such words include the following: (i) [mεmε] 'quickly' [meme] 'fastly' ... (iii) [dà2g] 'tail' [da2g] 'crocodile' / The examples below illustrate the distribution of tones in Koeneom Language / L + L [kàà] 'climb' ... H + H [tágbó] 'lizard' ... M + M [fuat] 'vomit' [paat] 'five' ... L + H [bìsá] 'food' ... L + H + L [làbárì] 'story'

new_statements.relation_note: new: nothing on record (Koenoem is not in the catalog and has no stress statement held by the project). This is a tone statement only (three level tones, contrastive); it makes no claim about word stress, so it neither places stress nor denies it. It is consistent with Blench 2016/2017 (Tal, the closest documented relative, has three level tones; A3 reconstructed with three level tones). Caution on reliability: Blench 2016 (work 1, txt l.264-266) says the Ilorin student dissertations on Pyapun/Koenoem 'contain high levels of disinformation'; this essay classifies Koenoem as Niger-Congo (txt l.300 area, sect. 1.3) and its named informants list Nupe, Igala and Gwarri as other languages spoken…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Koenoem is described as a tone language with three contrastive level (register) tones, High, Mid and Low, illustrated with tonal minimal pairs and with words of tone patterns L-L, H-H, M-M, L-H, L-H-L, L-H-L-H, L-L-H, H-H-H; contour tones are mentioned only in the general typology, not claimed for Koenoem. Nothing is said about word stress, accent or prominence in Koenoem: the phonology chapter covers consonants, vowels, tone and syllable structure (open syllables; CV, V, CVC with final nasal read as vowel nasalisation) only.

new_statements.identity_note: Oparemi 2011 describes 'Koenoem' located in Shendam LGA, Plateau State (chapter 1), i.e. the koen1239 language, from three informants via the Ibadan 400-wordlist; no dialect named (the essay mentions dialect differences between Koenoem groups without detail). Blench 2016 treats Koenoem (west of Pyapun, Talic subgroup with Tal and Pyapun; informants photographed at Koenoem, 2016) from his March-May 2016 survey wordlist; his phonology slides are on Tal, not Koenoem.

sources.note: Nothing. Section 6.2 'Phonology' (printed p. 10-11) gives only 'initial, cursory observations' (consonant and vowel inventories, labialization/palatalization, vowel length); no mention of stress, accent or word-level tone. Appendix E (printed p. 34) states: 'The transcriptions are preliminary since there was no in-depth analysis of tones or other phonological or phonetic features.' The 348-item wordlist is untoned.
